title: I bought a cheap studio three months into my first job. Too soon?
excerpt: A graduate from Sarawak signed for a RM200,000-plus studio near KL city centre three months into his first job. Sean says it was too soon, and sets out what he would do first at 23.

question.asker: From 874, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: The viewer is from Sarawak and started his first job in KL three months before writing. He has signed for a studio not far from KL city centre for a little over RM200,000, with a full loan at about 4.25% interest, hoping the rent will give positive cash flow and raise his loan eligibility for more units.
question.text: Is his interest rate fair, is this the right way to start, and should he have saved his first-home advantages for a better property?

answer.quote: Property is a very very slow game, but we can play very long.
answer.summary: Yes, it was too soon. He skipped the basics: an emergency fund, insurance, a stable career and comparing about 20 properties nearby. A cheap total price isn't the same as a good price per square foot. The interest rate matters less than these, since small loans to new borrowers usually carry higher rates.

reasons.title: Check the list before buying
reasons.body: First six months of living costs as an emergency fund, then medical insurance, then confidence that his job is stable and that he can live with a big loan. Only then compare the project's price per square foot with others around it.

reasons.title: Small, cheap units are a marketing trend
reasons.body: Developers sell units of about 450 sq ft for under RM250,000 near KLCC with promises of high Airbnb returns. Divided by the size, the price often isn't cheap at all.

reasons.title: Subsale first builds the next loan
reasons.body: A subsale can be rented out at once. After about six months the rent counts as income for the bank, raising loan eligibility instead of cutting it. The SPA also lets him withdraw from EPF Account 2 to help with the next purchase.

reasons.title: Your income drives the portfolio
reasons.body: Banks still need a strong active income before each new loan. Sean would spend his first years investing in his career and in people who can teach him, until his salary reaches about RM5,000.

actions: Build six months of emergency savings and buy a medical card before any purchase.
Get a credit card for essentials only, to build a credit record, and never treat the limit as savings.
Visit about 20 properties around any project and compare price per square foot.
Aim first for a subsale of RM300,000 to RM500,000 whose rent covers the instalment, then furnish and rent it out.
Use the second 90% loan on a new project, and expect later loans to need more cash.
caveat: Whether this purchase was right will only be clear once the project is completed and rented out. If it produces positive cash flow, it can still work.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #202. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in February 2023; loan margins and EPF withdrawal rules change, so check current ones. Sean mentions joining FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase group linked in the video description.
